A three-part sanctions law aimed at Iran, Russia, and North Korea. Its Russia title wrote existing executive order sanctions into statute and gave Congress the power to block the President from easing them.

::: {.official-links}
**Read the law** (official GovInfo text)

[Enacted text: Pub. L. 115-44](https://www.govinfo.gov/link/plaw/115/public/44){.btn-official} [Current U.S. Code: 22 U.S.C. 9401 et seq.](https://www.govinfo.gov/link/uscode/22/9401?link-type=html){.btn-official}
:::

## Key provisions

- Title I: sanctions on Iran's ballistic missile program and the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps.
- Sec. 216: congressional review, with a possible resolution of disapproval, before Russia sanctions are eased.
- Sec. 231: sanctions on anyone making a significant transaction with Russia's defense or intelligence sectors.
- Title III: North Korea sanctions on shipping, labor, and finance.

## Why it matters

Section 231 turned sanctions into an arms-transfer policy tool. It was applied to Turkey's defense procurement agency over the S-400 purchase and has shaped U.S. dealings with India, so it interacts with the [Arms Export Control Act](aeca-1976.qmd). Like the [Global Magnitsky Act](glomag-2016.qmd) it is carried out through [IEEPA](ieepa-1977.qmd).

## Current status

In force.
